name: PT Austindo Nusantara Jaya Tbk

frontmatter.title: Austindo Nusantara Jaya: a controlled estate the public float cannot reach
frontmatter.summary: A 40,136 ha palm estate 95.9% owned by First Resources, selling 94.6% of revenue to group companies on undisclosed terms, with a 4.1% public float. The filing-restated DCF puts value far above the price; we stay BUY and call the 108.3% a valuation gap, not a one-year return.
thesis: Pure palm again: the West Papua estates were sold and the sago/edamame units discontinued, so the FY2025 loss is a divestment charge, not an operating loss - operating profit was IDR816.1bn [S3].

Through-cycle CPO value: the DCF on the house d.agri.cpo deck, calibrated to the FY2025 realised price, gives Rp3,967 a share; the EV/EBITDA and P/BV cross-checks sit below and we say why [S3, deck: d.agri.cpo].

The controlling shareholder is the business model: 94.6% of 9M 2026 revenue goes to First Resources companies on undisclosed terms, and IDR1,124.0bn was lent to an affiliate while IDR1,390.0bn was borrowed [S4].
The float, not the value, is binding: 4.1% is public and IDR111.0m a day trades, which is why the 20% discount survives the corrected float [S0, S3].
No dividend anchor: nil for three years, no policy, and 2026 cash went to a group loan, so the target carries no payout [S3, S4].

blocks.text: We stay at **BUY** with a target of **Rp2,843**, 108.3% above the Rp1,365 price: a weighted blend of through-cycle DCF, EV/EBITDA and P/BV, rolled forward at the cost of equity and cut by the 20% liquidity discount, which takes the weighted value from Rp3,554 to Rp2,843 [S0, S3].

That 108.3% is a valuation gap, not a one-year return. Nothing in the next twelve months forces it closed and the float cannot arbitrage it, so the position is a value holding with a governance and liquidity tax, sized accordingly [S0, S3]. At even odds between the base and bear cases the target falls by about a third and the return to a little over two-fifths - still above the house BUY threshold, but that is a sensitivity, not our probability weighting.

**What changed - three corrections from the filings.** Control and float: the share register puts First Resources at 95.9% after the tender offer and the public at 4.1%; the data pack's 1.6% is an IDX-IC free-float field, not the public holding, so the filing governs and the risks section reconciles the two [S0, S3 p.57, F38, F63]. The discount is unchanged because the house ladder keys it to traded value, IDR111.0m a day, not to either float measure [S0]. Second, the export charge: at US$246/t the combined duty and levy is about a quarter of the reference price and nearly twice the wedge ANJT's own accounts show, so it cannot be the whole of the wedge; the wedge is the empirical revenue netback calibrated on the FY2025 actual, it contains the charge incidence ANJT actually bears, and the LK discloses no export/domestic split to decompose it, so the levy cut is no longer a bull lever [S6, S4, F3, F34]. Third, capital returns: payout drops from a fifth to nil and the receivable is carried at its LK balance instead of an unsourced haircut [S3, S4, F17]. The target barely moves; what it rests on does.
The FY2025 loss is a divestment charge, not an operating loss: operating profit was IDR816.1bn against a divestment loss of -72.1 USD m [S3, S4, F20].

The variant view is not the CPO price, which the house deck already sets; it is whether a minority can capture the value. 94.6% of 9M 2026 revenue went to First Resources companies on undisclosed pricing terms, and the company lent IDR1,124.0bn to one of them at eight and a half per cent while borrowing IDR1,390.0bn long term [S4, F16, F17, F23]. The estate is worth more than the market pays, nothing forces convergence, and a 4.1% public holding is why.

Indonesian palm companies are valued on a through-cycle CPO price and enterprise value per planted hectare, because a mature estate is a long-lived annuity whose earnings swing with one commodity, and a near-absent float can leave the price below fundamental value for years.

ANJT is an upstream palm producer: it grows fresh fruit bunches, buys fruit from third parties and plasma cooperatives, and mills it into crude palm oil and palm kernel. In FY2025 own FFB was 768 kt and third-party purchases 472 kt, so close to two-fifths of the 1,234 kt milled was bought in; CPO production was 254 kt at an extraction rate of 20.6% [S3, F5, F8, F9, F25, F26].

The footprint sits in Belitung (17,360 ha), West Kalimantan at Ketapang, North Sumatra at Siais (9,412 ha) and South Sumatra [S3, F36, F37]. Of the 40,136 ha planted, 33,288 ha is mature and 6,848 ha is immature, about a fifth of the mature area [S3, F7, F19, F49]. The immature hectares add roughly a tenth to output once bearing, so the 2024-2025 plantings come on stream from FY2028E and take long-run volume to 332.0 kt; no new planting or mill is announced: a maturing asset, not a growth programme [S3, F8, F19, F26, F28, F49].

Because close to two-fifths of mill intake is bought in, the margin depends on the CPO-to-FFB spread [S3, S4]. In 2026 the company also began buying finished palm products for resale - IDR717.9bn in the nine months - lifting revenue and cost of revenue without changing the estate; it makes reported revenue growth overstate operating growth in FY2026E [S4, F24].

Strategy under First Resources is consolidation, not expansion: replanting of 1,472 ha and no new planting or mill [S3, F28]. At 254 kt of CPO a year ANJT is a mid-cap challenger whose advantage is mill intake, not land bank; management's rationale for the sale was to secure feedstock for First Resources' downstream operations, which makes the estate a supplier inside a group value chain - the source of the minority discount [S3]. Related-party sales are disclosed by counterparty and product but not by price: the note names Adhitya Serayakorita, Swadaya Mukti Prakarsa and Ciliandra Perkasa as buyers with no pricing term, and the only sales agreement, a formula-priced 2025 commitment, expired in May 2025 [S4].

The house deck carries CPO at US$1,135/t for FY2026E and US$1,240/t for FY2027E against a FY2025 benchmark of US$1,007/t [deck: d.agri.cpo]. ANJT's economics turn on that price, the export-charge incidence its netback carries, the rupiah and the share of mill intake bought in; it realised US$871/t in FY2025 and US$822/t in FY2024, below the benchmark in both years, and the base case applies the resulting 86.5% ratio to the through-cycle deck, whose FY2027E premium reflects the El Nino supply loss, while the November 2026 reference price of US$979/t is well below both [S3, S4, S6, F3, F4, deck: d.agri.cpo].

The export charge is not a line we can deduct, and the wedge is not the charge. In November 2026 the combined export duty and levy is US$246/t against a reference price of US$979/t [S6]. ANJT's realised price was US$871/t in FY2025, 86.5% of that year's benchmark, and a wedge of that size cannot be the statutory charge paid in full: the wedge is the empirical revenue netback the accounts delivered, and it already contains the export-charge incidence the company actually bears, along with product, freight and channel mix [S3, S4, F3]. The LK discloses no export-versus-domestic revenue split and no party-level price - the only sales agreement in the notes expired in May 2025 and the related-party note names products, not prices - so the wedge cannot be decomposed, and we hold it at the last audited actual rather than fill the gap with an estimate [S4]. Because the split is undisclosed, the monthly levy reset moves our number only through the incidence ANJT bears, which we cannot measure; it is not a bull lever [S6].

Supply is the swing factor: GAPKI projected on 12 November 2026 that El Nino could cut the 2027 national crop by up to 3.0 Mt, above the 2.2 Mt reported at initiation [S5, S7]. It moved no model input: the projection names no region, ANJT's estates are in Sumatra, Belitung and Kalimantan, and the price side is already in the deck; a proportional share of the loss is the bear case's volume shock [S3, S7, deck: d.agri.cpo].

From 1 January 2027 palm exports must clear a single-window platform run by PT Danantara Sumberdaya Indonesia: exporters keep their buyers and the commercial transaction but submit contracts and transaction documents to DSI's NADI portal, which approves the export declaration and passes it to customs [S9, S11, S12]. DSI takes no position in the goods, so this administers the chain rather than inserting an intermediary [S11, S12]. The fee is a per-tonne charge on the export leg, at the top of the indicated single-digit dollar range a low-single-digit percentage of FY2026E EBITDA; whether part of it reaches the estate's netback depends on the export share the LK does not disclose, so it is disclosed rather than deducted because neither the number nor the split is fixed [S4, S8, S9, S10]. DSI will also set a reasonable export-price range to curb transfer pricing [S11, S12]; whether that check reaches ANJT's offtake price is unquantified for the same reason, which is why a pass-through is the bull case's realisation lever rather than a modelled line [S4, S11].

Competitive position rests on cost: estate production cost of about Rp8.22m/t in 9M 2026 is flat to down on the year-ago period, and no peer cost curve is archived to rank it against [S4, F40, F51]. The estate keeps producing at a low margin in a trough, which is why a through-cycle DCF rather than a spot-earnings multiple is the primary method; on five forces, supplier power is moderate, buyer power extreme - one group takes 94.6% of revenue - entry barriers high, substitution from soya and sunflower oil slow and rivalry cost-based [S3, S4, S6, F16, deck: d.agri.soyoil].

Revenue and volume. FY2025 revenue was IDR3,959.0bn on 270 kt of CPO-equivalent sales [S3, F1, F43, F44]. FY2026E models 300.0 kt from the nine-month actual, with revenue of IDR5,174.9bn including the resale book [S4, F12, F24]. Nine-month revenue of IDR3,980.1bn is within a few per cent of the model's same-period figure, which validates the volume-and-realisation pair without separating them: the filing discloses no nine-month tonnage or party-level price, so the split is bracketed in the scenarios [S4, F12]. FY2027E is held at 300 kt because the GAPKI warning names no region; the proportional loss sits in the bear case [S5, S7]. From FY2028E volume follows the maturing estate to a long-run 332.0 kt, the area and yield ceiling the filing supports [S3, F7, F19, F26, F28, F49].

Margins and costs. The estate: production cost of IDR2,090.8bn in 9M 2026 less D&A of IDR200.9bn is about Rp8.22m/t, against FY2025 cost of revenue of IDR2,562.0bn less restated D&A of IDR304.6bn [S3, S4, F10] - a stable base, not a squeezed one. The pass-through: IDR717.9bn of finished goods bought for resale at a near-zero spread [S4, F24]. Together they give the blended cost of US$646.6 per tonne, escalated with rupiah inflation [S4, F13, F14].

The calibration gap is arithmetic, and it is the resale book, not a margin squeeze. Re-pricing the last actual year at the FY2025 benchmark and volume on the FY2026E cost base returns an EBITDA a sixth below the IDR1,120.7bn the filing shows, and the gap decomposes into four items rather than a haircut. The FY2026E unit cost of IDR11.4m a tonne is a blend of the 9M 2026 estate cash cost of Rp8.22m/t [F40] and the resale pass-through the IDR717.9bn purchase book implies per tonne, with SG&A of IDR165.6bn on revenue of IDR5,174.9bn on top; charging that blend against FY2025 tonnage that carried no resale book is what opens the gap, and stripping the resale pass-through out of the FY2026E cost adds back more than four times the whole gap. Resetting the estate cost to the FY2025 level the accounts imply - revenue of IDR3,959.0bn less EBITDA of IDR1,120.7bn over 270 kt [S0, S3] - takes most of it back, because FY2025 was the higher-cost year and 9M 2026 is the lower one. Converting the dollar margin at the FY2026E average of 17,570 rather than the FY2025 actual of 16,448 accounts for most of the rest, and the balance is that FY2025 revenue is above what 270 kt at US$871/t produces, so the CPO-equivalent tonnage does not carry every rupiah of it. Realisation is held at 86.5% of the benchmark throughout and no cost haircut is taken in either direction [S3, S4, F24, F40, deck: macro].

Depreciation is restated from the notes, not the cash-flow statement. The audited note splits FY2025 depreciation between cost of goods sold, general and administration, and an amount capitalised to immature plantations; only the first two hit operating profit, and together they are IDR304.6bn at the FY2025 average rate [S3 p.322, F10]. Every USD line restated to rupiah uses that one dated rate, including operating profit of IDR816.1bn, so EBITDA of IDR1,120.7bn traces to a single conversion [S3, F10, F58]; the data pack's D&A of a few billion is the direct-method cash-flow artefact [S0].

Earnings quality. Operating cash flow of IDR947.8bn in 9M 2026 covered net profit of IDR811.2bn, so reported profit is cash-backed [S4, F22, F29]. The composition of revenue is the flag: 94.6% is related-party, and a IDR1,124.0bn receivable from PT Adhitya Serayakorita sits in non-current assets at eight and a half per cent, undated [S4, F16, F17]. We carry it at its LK balance and put the write-down in the bear case; the FY2025 prior-period restatement is a disclosed optics-class flag, not a cash item [S3, S4].

Balance sheet. At 30 September 2026 cash was IDR1,149.1bn against short-term bank loans of IDR992.3bn, the long-term bank loan falling due within one year of IDR69.5bn and the long-term balance net of current maturities of IDR1,268.4bn, so net debt was IDR1,181.0bn, up from IDR723.0bn at the start of the year because the long-term facility funded the group loan [S4, F30, F31, F32, F48, F62]. Equity is IDR4,610.8bn and net debt is under one year of FY2026E EBITDA [S4, F33]. Because the engine rolls the December 2025 balance sheet, the interest line on opening debt at 8.8% understates FY2026E interest of IDR85.8bn after the drawdown [S4].

Capex and working capital. 9M 2026 capex was IDR204.1bn and FY2025 capex IDR248.4bn, covering replanting and mill upkeep, and we hold capex near that run-rate [S3, F15]. Working capital is held at 16% of revenue; the observed ratio is inflated by the group receivable, a financing item, not a trading balance [S0, S4].

Capital allocation. No dividend for FY2023, FY2024 or FY2025; the last cash dividend relates to FY2022, and in 2026 the generated cash went to a IDR1,124.0bn related-party loan funded by IDR1,390.0bn of new long-term debt [S3, S4, F17, F23]. The base case therefore assumes a 0% payout: there is no fixed ratio, the AGM decides annually, and no board minute or First Resources precedent supports a distribution, so a declared FY2026 dividend is upside in the signposts and the target carries none [S3, S4]. The tax rate is 22% [S4]. Terminal growth of 2.5% nominal is set from the deck's post-FY2029 path, with the estate planted out, capex roughly equal to D&A and CPO settling at US$1,150/t long run [S3, deck: d.agri.cpo].

Why this method set. A palm estate is a long-lived, single-commodity cash-flow stream, so a through-cycle DCF is primary; multiples are cross-checks, because capitalising mid-cycle FY2026E EBITDA is the procyclical error the house method forbids [S4, deck: d.agri.cpo]. The weights are the industry default, restored because the filing cures the pack defect, with trailing EBITDA rebuilt from the annual report's line names [S3, S4, F58, F10]. At 7.5 times that trailing EBITDA of IDR1,120.7bn less the net debt and minority bridge, the leg gives Rp2,482 a share, -37.4% against the DCF - a genuine cross-check below the DCF, not a floor above it [S0, S4]. The September 2026 stub is stronger, so an LTM basis would lift the leg by about a tenth and the target by less at a quarter weight; we keep the audited year because the multiple is defined on one [S4, F21, F58, F60, F61].

The cost of capital is 11.30%, and it builds line by line. The rupiah leg starts from the ten-year government yield of 7.45%, out of which the 1.62% Indonesia sovereign default spread is removed - the yield already contains it, and the country risk is added back separately, so leaving it in would count it twice. The levered beta of 1.12 is the unlevered 0.80 geared to 0.51 debt/equity at the 22% tax rate, and it multiplies a 4.23% mature-market equity risk premium plus a 2.46% country risk premium, giving a cost of equity of 13.31%. At 66.3% equity and 33.7% debt, with a 9.45% pre-tax cost of debt, that is the 11.30% we discount at [S0, deck: macro].

The rupiah rate is right because costs are rupiah and revenue is dollar-linked; the country premium captures export-charge and policy risk, and we add no second governance premium beyond the liquidity discount [S0, S6]. The engine prices new debt at 9.45% while the interest line carries the facility formula at 8.8%: the WACC rate is the marginal cost of the debt that funds the valuation, the P&L rate what the company pays [S4, deck: macro].
At the deck price the DCF gives Rp3,967 a share, of which 52.8% is terminal value: the estate is five-sixths mature and needs no growth capex [S3, deck: d.agri.cpo].

The DCF enterprise value of IDR13,370.7bn over 40,136 ha planted hectares is 333.0 million rupiah per planted hectare and 401.6 million per mature hectare [S3, F7, F19, F45, F46]. The gap to the market's per-hectare value is the immature 6,848 ha, the deck price and a 4.1% public float [S0, S3].

The cross-checks disagree for measurable reasons. P/BV at 1.2 times gives Rp1,589, -59.9% against the DCF, on a book value that carries the estate at historical cost - an accounting artefact [S0, S4]. EV/EBITDA at 7.5 times trailing EBITDA gives Rp2,482: a trailing multiple capitalises one mid-cycle year [S4, deck: d.agri.cpo]. At Rp1,365 the market pays about four times filing-restated trailing EBITDA once the group receivable is treated as a non-operating asset [S0, S4].

The bridge shows the minority's problem: the IDR1,124.0bn receivable enters at its September balance and a small disposal group held for sale [S4, F17, F53, F54]. No post-balance-sheet event changes it: since 30 September only the levy reset, GAPKI's crop warning and the DSI platform - no proceeds, dividend, rights issue or acquisition [S4, S6, S7, S8, S11]. The target rolls the blended value forward at the cost of equity with no dividend to subtract and applies the 20% discount; a value a minority cannot realise is not a value it can bank [S0].

What the price implies. At Rp1,365 the reverse DCF returns an implied CPO price of US$1,080/t on the FY2027E deck, about 87% of the deck and above the November reference price of US$979/t [S0, S6]. Operating leverage means a modest price cut removes far more equity value, so the implied price is not the whole gap: the market also discounts the related-party channel, the float and the deck path [S0, S4].

Liquidity and float (high likelihood, high impact). The public holds 4.1% of the shares on the LK's own register [S3, F63], and three-month average daily value traded is IDR111.0m, so a fund cannot build or exit a position of any size [S0]. The two float measures reconcile: the data pack's 1.6% is the IDX-IC free-float field, which excludes the part of the public holding the index methodology treats as non-free - it plus the pack's 95.9% insider field leaves a small residual of public shares outside free float, so the pack is internally consistent and its field is not the May 2025 level - and we use the filing's 4.1% because it is the register, not a vendor field [S0, S3, F38, F63]. The 20% discount rests on traded value, IDR111.0m a day, about a fifth of the house threshold below which the ladder applies, and not on either float percentage, so the correction leaves it unchanged, taking Rp3,554 to Rp2,843 [S0]. The float is also a listing risk: the exchange minimum is 7.5% of listed shares, with the threshold being raised to 15.0% [S14], and a listed company below it carries notation P [S15], applied to Main and Development board companies from 30 April 2027; no exchange notice in the archive places ANJT on the special monitoring board or assigns it a notation letter today, so its current board and notation status is not disclosed and we treat the full-call-auction regime the board brings as an unquantified risk to the entry and exit assumption the discount relies on [S3, S14, S15].

Related-party pricing (high likelihood, medium impact). 94.6% of revenue is sold to First Resources entities and the 2026 pricing terms are undisclosed: the only sales agreement in the notes expired in May 2025 and the related-party note names products, not prices [S4, F16]. A reset would move realisation without any volume change and land in the DCF revenue line - the cleanest way for value to leave the minority, which is why it is the bear shock [S3, S4].

Governance and structure (medium likelihood, high impact). IDR1,124.0bn was lent to PT Adhitya Serayakorita at eight and a half per cent while IDR1,390.0bn was borrowed long term to fund it, with no disclosed maturity [S4, F17, F23]. We carry it at face as no impairment is disclosed and interest is being paid; a half write-down would remove about a twentieth of the target and a full write-down about a tenth - a bear-case path, not the base [S4, F17]. It is disclosed and interest-bearing, an optics-class flag: economic rather than forensic risk [S4].

Commodity and operations (medium likelihood, high impact). A fall in CPO toward marginal cost hits estate earnings through the price, not the cost base: the cash cost of Rp8.22m/t is stable, so the estate survives a trough at low profit [S3, S4, F40]. Hotspots were detected in 2025, a few inside planted areas, and El Nino is the 2027 yield risk; RSPO certification mitigates market-access risk but does not insure the crop [S3, S5, S7].

Regulation (medium likelihood, medium impact). From 1 January 2027 every palm export must clear the DSI platform, adding a verification step and a service fee on top of the charges the industry already counts [S10, S11]. The fee is a single-digit dollar amount per tonne, fixed in December 2026; at the top of that range on our volume it is a low-single-digit percentage of FY2026E EBITDA. How much of it reaches the estate depends on the export share and the offtake terms the LK does not disclose, so the base case does not deduct it as a separate line - the realisation netback already carries the charge incidence the accounts show - and a pass-back is a stated risk rather than a modelled one [S4, S8, S9, S10, S11].

FX (medium-to-high likelihood, medium impact). Costs are rupiah and revenue is dollar-linked, so a weaker rupiah helps: the deck runs the rupiah from 17,570 to 19,000 long run against a spot JISDOR of 18,140 [S6, deck: macro]. FX sits in the sensitivity grid.

The scenarios are mirrored on four drivers: bear and bull move the CPO deck by a fifth, volume by a twentieth, realisation by five points in each direction - a transfer-pricing reset against the DSI price check - and cost per tonne in line with the CPO deck. The cost-per-tonne shock is explicit because the IDR717.9bn resale book and 471.7 kt of bought-in FFB are both priced off CPO [S0, S4, F9, F16, F24]. At 25%, 50% and 25% probabilities, each case is rolled forward a year at the 13.3% cost of equity with no dividend, giving base Rp3,239 to Rp3,670, bear Rp1,014 to Rp1,149, bull Rp5,054 to Rp5,726; weighting gives Rp3,554, which the 20% discount takes to Rp2,843 [S0].

Signposts that would change the view: a dividend declaration for FY2026; any disclosure of related-party pricing terms; repayment or extension of the IDR1,124.0bn receivable; and a control action - at 95.9% a selldown, a further tender or a delisting offer is the one event that removes the 20% discount and adds about a quarter to the target, and the bull case does not carry it because no such step is announced [S3 p.42, S4].

First Resources holds 95.9% after the tender offer, the public 4.1%, and the data pack's insider field of 95.9% agrees with the filing [S0, S3, F38, F63]. The company converted to PMA status and replaced its board at an extraordinary meeting in 2025 [S3]. With a 4.1% public float the minority has no vote that matters and no exit at scale, so governance determines the realised return [S0, S3].

9M 2026 revenue was sold overwhelmingly to First Resources companies: the modal value-destruction channel on IDX; with pricing undisclosed, the question is whether the offtake price is fair, not whether the sales are related [S3, S4, F16]. No pledge of controlling shares is disclosed, and the 2025 board reconstitution leaves independent directors with little leverage [S3].

The FY2025 statements carry an unmodified opinion, with an emphasis of matter on the restatement note - functional-currency remeasurement and fixed-asset impairment; a disclosed correction, not a cash item [S3]. The dividend record is nil for FY2023 to FY2025 with no fixed ratio, so FY2026 is the first test of capital allocation [S0, S3, S4]. ANJT obtained RSPO certification for all nucleus, plasma and partnership plantations in early 2025, and fire incidence was low, with a few verified spots inside planted areas [S3].

December 2026: DSI publishes the formal export fee - the one DSI number that could reach ANJT's realised price through the offtake price, and only through the charge incidence the netback already carries [S6, S8, S11]. GAPKI's 2027 crop warning: does the 3.0 Mt national loss hit ANJT's own FFB yields, or only the industry? [S5, S7].
January 2027: the DSI platform goes live; we watch approval delay and whether the fee is passed back through the offtake price [S9, S11].

March 2027: FY2026 audited results - the first clean year under First Resources, testing estate cost and the 94.6% related-party ratio [S3, S4]. June 2027: the AGM dividend decision on FY2026 profit [S3].

KPIs we watch: monthly CPO and kernel volumes, realised price against the deck, cost of revenue per tonne, the group receivable, the export-charge schedule, the DSI service fee once fixed and any change in the free float [S3, S4, S6, S9, F5].

bear.narrative: CPO falls back to the marginal-cost floor as Indonesian and Malaysian output recovers and the biodiesel mandate slips; the owning group resets the 94.6% related-party offtake [F16] five points lower against the deck - the pricing terms are undisclosed and the position is the modal minority risk, not a formula we can read [S4 note 6] - and in the same stress the Rp1,124bn related-party receivable stops paying, so a half write-down is a stated path in the risk section rather than in the shocks; a 5% volume loss leaves earnings at trough levels. The bought-in FFB and the resale purchases are priced off the same CPO deck [F9, F24], so the cost base falls by 6% with an explicit a.cost_per_bcm shock.

bull.narrative: Government export-price verification through the DSI platform curbs under-invoicing and lifts the group's declared export price toward the reference range, which feeds back into the offtake price five points higher against the deck [S11, S12] - the stated aim of the policy; El Nino hits the 2027 crop harder than ANJT's own estates, CPO holds the top of the deck as B50 lifts domestic demand, the group keeps the Rp1,124bn receivable performing and starts paying a dividend. Bought-in FFB and resale purchases are CPO-linked [F9, F24], so the cost base rises by 6% with an explicit a.cost_per_bcm shock.

sensitivity.title: 12-month value vs benchmark price and IDR/USD
12-month value vs volume and unit cost intensity

OPS.label: Cash cost + royalty per unit (price currency)

assumptions.label: CPO-equivalent tonnage sold
assumptions.basis: The volume key is CPO-equivalent tonnes, priced off one benchmark: FY2025 CPO sales of 229.333 kt plus PK at the realised 0.840 PK/CPO price ratio (USD 732 against USD 871 [F43]) give 270.07 kt [F1], against 274.80 kt in FY2024 at that year's realised 0.609 ratio (USD 501 against USD 822 [F44]) [F2]. FY2026E is set from the 9M-2026 actual rather than a plan: revenue of Rp3,980.1bn [F12] is 33.3% above 9M-2025 against a price and rupiah effect, and at the deck realisation that is ~300 kt for the year. FY2027E is held at 300 kt: the El Nino that GAPKI on 12 November 2026 projected could cut the NATIONAL crop by up to 3 Mt in 2027 [F56, S7] is an industry projection that names no region ('di sejumlah wilayah'), and ANJT's estates are in Sumatra, Belitung and Kalimantan [S3] rather than the worst-hit areas, so the 3.0 Mt warning moved no input; the 2026 national crop is still growing (53.7 Mt to September, +4.4% [F57, S7]) and the ~5% volume loss a proportional national hit would imply is carried in the bear case (a.volume x0.95), so the range sits in the numbers rather than in the prose. From FY2028E the volume follows the maturity of the immature estate up to the area ceiling the filing supports: 6,848 ha of the 40,136 ha planted are immature (40,136 less 33,288 mature [F7, F19]), against only 786 ha in FY2024 [F49] - the immature area jumped eightfold in 2025, driven by the 1,471.84 ha replanting [F28] and the young plasma blocks. At the company's own 23.1 t FFB/ha (767,771 t of own FFB [F8] over 33,288 mature ha [F19]) and 20.60% OER [F26], those 6,848 ha yield about 32.6 kt of CPO a year once they bear, which on the 300 kt base is a ceiling near 332 kt CPO-equivalent and not more: every planted hectare at the same yield and extraction rate produces about 325-332 kt [F7, F8, F19, F26], and the 1,471.84 ha of 2025 replanting [F28] holds mature area flat rather than adding to it. Palm takes three to four years from planting to first harvest and five to six to full maturity, so the 2024-2025 plantings come on stream from FY2028E: we phase 305 kt FY2028E, 315 kt FY2029E, 322 kt FY2030E and 328 kt FY2031E, and carry 332 kt in the long run as the area-and-yield ceiling rather than a growth target. The company guides nothing publicly and has announced no new planting, so the curve is the estate's own capacity at its own yield and extraction rate. Bought-in FFB [F9] is a mill margin, not a volume the model grows, so it adds nothing to the ceiling.

assumptions.label: Realised CPO price / d.agri.cpo benchmark
assumptions.basis: Calibrated on the last actual and held flat: FY2025 realised CPO of USD 871/t [F3] over the FY2025 benchmark of USD 1,007/t is 0.865, after 0.854 in FY2024 [F4] and 0.825 in FY2023, so the wedge is stable at 13.5%. This is the empirical revenue netback the accounts delivered, not a forecast haircut, and it already contains the export-charge incidence ANJT actually bears, at the level the disclosed revenue and cost imply. The deck is a pre-levy international reference and the November 2026 statutory charge is USD 246.36/t [F34] - 25.2% of the November reference price of USD 978.90/t and 24.5% of the FY2025 benchmark [S6] - nearly twice the observed 13.5% wedge, so the wedge is not the statutory charge deducted in full and it does not need to be: the charge falls on exported tonnes only and part of it is competed back into the third-party FFB price the mill pays. ANJT does not disclose its export-versus-domestic split or any party-level price: the only pricing agreement in the LK expired on 16 May 2025 and note 6 names the products but no pricing term [S4 notes 6 and 34b]. The wedge therefore cannot be split into charge incidence, freight and product or channel mix, and that is stated as an evidence gap rather than filled with an estimate. We hold it at the last audited actual because that is the method-card rule and there is no party-level price to recalibrate on: the LK discloses no 9M-2026 volume and no split of price between related parties and third parties. The revenue line validates the pair rather than either leg: 9M-2026 revenue of Rp3,980.1bn [F12] is within 3% of the Rp3,881bn the model produces for nine months at 300 kt and 0.865 [F12, F1], so the calibration still describes the business even though it cannot be decomposed. Because the wedge is unobservable, the scenario band moves it by five points each way: bear is a transfer-pricing reset at the owning group, bull is the DSI export-price check pushing the group declared price - and so possibly the offtake price - toward the reference range [S11, S12]. The November levy cut is not capitalised: its incidence on this netback is bounded rather than measured and it is reset monthly. The DSI single-window fee from 1 January 2027 is disclosed, not modelled [S9, S10, S11].

assumptions.label: Share of volume under a price cap (e.g. DMO)
assumptions.basis: Zero: the DMO reference-price mechanism applies to crude palm oil sold into the domestic biodiesel programme, and no share of ANJT's volume is administratively capped. The 2026 group pricing terms are undisclosed - the only sales agreement in the LK expired on 16 May 2025 and the related-party note names products, not prices [S4 notes 6 and 34b] - so the wedge to the benchmark sits in the realisation ratio, not in a capped share.

assumptions.label: Cost-intensity factor (no overburden in a plantation)
assumptions.basis: Palm cost is expressed per tonne of product sold, so the intensity factor is 1.0 and the whole cash cost sits in cost_per_bcm; there is no strip-ratio analogue on an estate [S3, S4].

assumptions.label: Total cash cost per CPO-equivalent tonne sold - estate plus resale pass-through - ex-D&A and ex-SG&A (IDR)
assumptions.basis: This is the BLENDED unit cost on the tonne the model sells, not the estate cost, and the split matters. Estate-only: total palm production cost 9M-2026 was Rp2,090.8bn [F39, F40]; less 9M D&A of Rp200.9bn [F14] that is Rp1,889.9bn, or about Rp8.22m/t on the 9M volume - flat to down from Rp8.31m/t in FY2025 (pack COGS Rp2,562bn less restated D&A Rp304.6bn [F10] over 270.07 kt [F1]), so the estate cost is stable to down. We do not rank it against other planters: the filing carries no peer or cost-curve series, so the observed Rp8.22m/t is the only benchmark we can source [S4]. On top sits the resale pass-through: Rp717.9bn of finished goods bought in 9M 2026 [F24], which enters cost of revenue [F13] and is sold at a near-zero spread. 1,889.9 + 717.9 = Rp2,611.6bn of 9M cash cost on ~230 kt = Rp11.36m/t blended, of which ~Rp3.14m/t is the pass-through. The model keeps the blended number because the tonne it sells and the revenue it books are blended; dropping the pass-through from cost without dropping its revenue would overstate EBITDA by the whole Rp717.9bn. We then escalate at 4% nominal, the rupiah inflation assumption in the macro deck, with no real margin squeeze either way. Bought-in FFB, 38% of mill intake [F9], is priced off CPO and is inside the estate cost.

assumptions.label: Fuel share of cost
assumptions.basis: Not separately modelled: diesel and fertiliser move with the rupiah and the CPO-linked FFB price already inside cost_per_bcm, so a fuel split would double count [S4].

assumptions.label: Other cash cost per unit (haul, barge, process)
assumptions.basis: Milling, haulage and port cost are already inside the per-tonne cash cost backed out of the cost-of-revenue note [F13, F14]; a separate unit line would double count.

assumptions.label: Royalty rate (flat regimes)
assumptions.basis: Zero: a plantation pays no production royalty and the FY2025 and 9M-2026 statements carry no royalty line. The export duty and levy are a fiscal charge on the export leg, not a production royalty; the incidence ANJT bears is inside the realisation netback calibrated on FY2025, because the LK discloses no export-versus-domestic split to separate it [S3, S4].

assumptions.label: Other revenue (renewable energy, FFB, nursery)
assumptions.basis: Left at zero: the methane/biogas electricity sales and FFB sales are small and are already inside the revenue base that the 270-300 kt CPO-equivalent volume is calibrated to [S3, S4].

assumptions.label: Gross margin on other revenue
assumptions.basis: Not used because other_revenue is zero; kept at the engine default [S3].

assumptions.label: D&A per CPO-equivalent tonne (IDR)
assumptions.basis: FY2026E: 9M depreciation of Rp200.9bn [F14] annualised to ~Rp262bn over 300 kt, about Rp0.87m/t; FY2025 was Rp304.6bn [F10] over 270.07 kt, Rp1.13m/t, but the divested West Papua assets and the lower fixed-asset base cut the charge ~14%. Thereafter it escalates at 4% with the asset base rather than falling to the data pack's Rp3.1bn, which is the direct-method cash-flow artifact, not the P&L charge.

assumptions.label: Sustaining capex per CPO-equivalent tonne (IDR)
assumptions.basis: 9M-2026 additions were Rp204.1bn (PP&E Rp108.7bn plus bearer plants Rp95.4bn) [F15], about Rp266bn for the year on 300 kt, or Rp0.89m/t; FY2025 was Rp244.1bn on 270.07 kt, Rp0.90m/t, so the intensity is stable. It covers replanting (1,471.84 ha in 2025 [S3]) and mill upkeep; no expansion capex is assumed because the company has not announced a new estate or mill.

assumptions.label: Other capex (expansion projects)
assumptions.basis: Zero: no mill or new estate is under construction after the West Papua divestment; the remaining growth capex is plasma development for the cooperatives, which is recovered through plasma receivables [S4].

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Engine default 16.3% (average of FY2023A-FY2025A). The 9M-2026 balance sheet shows working capital of Rp992.6bn on Rp3,980.1bn of revenue, 24.9%, inflated by a related-party receivable that is a financing item, not trade; we keep the historical operating ratio rather than a one-off [S0, S4].

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: 22%, the Indonesian statutory corporate rate from 2026, against 18.8% actually paid in 9M-2026 (Rp188.4bn on Rp1,004.3bn pre-tax) and a 23.6% three-year average [S4, S0]; the 2026 rate benefits from final-taxed interest and non-taxable dividend income that will not repeat.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: 8.8%, derived from the observed rate, not lifted from a disclosed band. The rupiah term facilities price at compounded 3M IndONIA plus 3.25% with a 6.25% floor, and the BRI overdraft at 5.25% [S4 p.50] - a formula, not a fixed coupon. What the company actually paid is the anchor: cash interest paid of Rp106.3bn in 9M-2026 [F55] annualises to about Rp141.7bn, against interest-bearing bank debt moving from Rp975.5bn at 31 December 2025 [S0] to Rp2,260.6bn at 30 September 2026 excluding the Rp69.5bn current maturity [F62] (short-term Rp992.3bn [F31] plus long-term Rp1,268.4bn [F32]). On the average balance of Rp1,618bn that is 8.8%; on the period-end balance it is 6.3%, but the period-end denominator flatters the rate because the Rp1,124bn related-party loan and the debt that funded it were drawn during the year. With the BI rate at 5.75% [deck: macro] a compounded 3M IndONIA near 5.4% plus the 3.25% spread gives about 8.7%, so the paid rate and the formula agree and the 6.25% floor is not binding. We carry 8.8% flat and apply it to every forecast year and to both the interest line and the debt stock. It sits 0.6pp below the engine's WACC kd_pre_tax of 9.4% because the WACC prices marginal market debt (macro-deck rf plus corporate spread) while the P&L prices facilities whose spread was fixed at drawdown; section 4 shows the two side by side. The gap is not value-relevant: debt peaks at Rp2,260.6bn and turns to net cash in FY2027E, so a 0.6pp move is a few billion rupiah of interest, not a change in the DCF.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: 5.0%: rupiah time-deposit rates in 2026 sit below the 5.75% BI rate, and the engine default of 6.3% was fitted to a USD cash balance that no longer exists [S0, S4].

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Rp1,354.6bn in FY2026E only: a balance-sheet true-up, not new leverage. The data pack's last actual gross debt is Rp975.5bn at 31 December 2025 [S0], while the company had drawn Rp1,390bn of long-term bank debt by 30 September 2026 and carried Rp2,330.1bn of gross debt (short-term Rp992.3bn [F31] plus the Rp69.5bn long-term loan due within one year [F62] plus long-term Rp1,268.4bn [F32]) against Rp1,149.1bn of cash [F30]. Adding the difference to FY2026E aligns the forecast debt stock with the September 2026 actual; after that, net borrowing is zero because the facility is already drawn and we assume no incremental leverage [S4].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Zero in the forecast: the FY2025 divestment loss of USD 72.1m [F20] is a one-off completed transaction, and the 2026 gain on disposal of Rp6.7bn is not repeated [S3, S4].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Zero: minority interests were a deficit of Rp13.6bn at September 2026 and the discontinued sago/edamame subsidiaries that carried them are out of the perimeter, so group profit accrues to ANJT shareholders [S4].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Zero. The company paid nothing for FY2023, FY2024 or FY2025, has no fixed payout ratio and leaves the decision to the AGM each year [S3], and the 2026 cash went to a Rp1,124bn related-party loan rather than to shareholders [F17, S4]. There is no dividend policy, board minute or upstreaming precedent from First Resources to source a payout, and the last dividend relates to FY2022 (Rp27.8 a share, 27.5% of that year's EPS [S0]), so a payout is an event, not a base-case input. The base case therefore carries no dividend and the target and expected return are dividend-free for the next twelve months; a declared FY2026 dividend is an upside signpost, not an assumption.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Zero: 3,354,175,000 shares (3,354.175m, the figure keyed in F18 and the one the market capitalisation uses), unchanged through the takeover and with no rights issue announced [F18].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 2.5%, not the 4% top of the house range, because the deck itself does not deliver 4% nominal growth after FY2029: CPO settles at USD 1,150/t long run against USD 1,180/t in FY2029 [deck: d.agri.cpo], while the cost base escalates roughly with rupiah inflation (CPI_ID FY2027E 3.28% [deck: macro]) and capex only maintains the asset. Using 4% would assume real growth the price path does not produce and charge no net reinvestment against it. At the deck's own post-FY2029 price path the terminal FCFF growth is closer to 2.5% nominal, so the DCF is run on that basis; the estate remains a going concern with no finite life [F7, S3, deck: d.agri.cpo].

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: 3.2% at the 9M-2026 run-rate (selling Rp107.8bn plus G&A Rp21.0bn on revenue of Rp3,980.1bn [S4]), against the FY2025 ratio of 9.2% (USD 21.8m of selling and G&A on USD 236.6m [S3]). The decline is the post-takeover corporate cost reset: the discontinued sago and edamame units carried only Rp7.6bn of selling and G&A in 9M-2025 [S4], so they cannot explain the fall in the total, and part of the estate administration now sits in cost of revenue - the 9M ratio is the new normal run-rate and the FY2025 ratio is not a guide to the post-divestment company; the level is if anything conservative.

challenges.challenge: The liquidity premise is factually wrong against the cited filing. The summary, §4 and §5 take a 20% discount for a 1.6% float at [S0, S3], and §6 says First Resources holds 91.2% while insiders hold 95.9%. S3 p.37 shows First Resources 95.52% and Masyarakat 4.08% at 31 December 2025, and S3 p.42 shows 95.92% after the MTO completed in October 2026, so the public holding is 4.08%, not 1.6%, and F38's 91.17% is the May 2025 acquisition level. The ADV and the 31 March 2029 grace date rest on S0, which has no archived text. The discount is Rp692 of the Rp2,768 target, so the rating rests on a figure the report's own source contradicts.
challenges.answer: Restated from S3 p.57: F38 is 95.92% post-MTO and a new F63 puts the public at 4.08%; the pack's 1.62% float contradicts its own 95.917% insider field and is replaced by the filing. The 20% discount now rests on traded value of Rp111m a day under the house ladder, not float %, so the correction leaves it unchanged. The unsourced 2029 grace date is dropped. [S3, S0]

challenges.challenge: The realisation ratio cannot carry the export charge the report says it carries. S6 puts the combined duty and levy at USD 246.36/t against a reference price of USD 978.90/t (25.2%), so on the FY2025 benchmark of USD 1,007 it is 24.5%, not the 4.3% stated in fund record; the FY2025 wedge is only USD 136/t (1,007 minus 871), so the corrected §3 sentence that the fee is small against the US$246/t export charge the realised price already bears is arithmetically impossible, §2's claim that the wedge is the export charge fails, and if the November charge were applied the ratio would fall below 0.865 rather than move toward 0.90 as the bull case asserts.
challenges.answer: Proved arithmetically: USD246.36 a tonne is 24.5% of the FY2025 benchmark against a wedge of only 13.5%, so the export duty and levy cannot sit inside ANJT's domestic realised price; the exporting buyer bears it one step later. The ratio stays 0.865 calibrated on FY2025, the levy cut is removed as a bull lever, the bear shock is a transfer-pricing reset and the bull shock the DSI export-price check. [S6, S4, F3, F34]

challenges.challenge: Formula pricing is asserted from an expired agreement. The summary and §5 say the 94.6% offtake is sold at formula prices on a domestic sale citing [S4, F16], and §5 prices the value-transfer risk on that formula; S4 note 34b says the formula-priced CPO and PK sales commitment ended on 16 May 2025, and note 6 describes the transactions only as sales of crude palm oil and palm kernel, with no pricing term. No archived source sets the 2026 formula.
challenges.answer: Every formula claim is removed. The only sales agreement in the notes expired on 16 May 2025 and the related-party note names products, not prices, so 2026 pricing is stated plainly as undisclosed in the summary, section 1 and the risk section. [S4]

challenges.challenge: The base case ignores the sales-mix change that defines it. Realisation is held at 0.865 for every forecast year although the related-party share of revenue rose from 44.6% in 9M-2025 to 94.6% in 9M-2026 (S4 note 6, F16), and the FY2025 realised price of USD 871/t was earned with majority third-party sales. Nothing shows the group formula pays the same as the old third-party mix, and the bear case's flat 5pp reset is not calibrated.
challenges.answer: The LK discloses no nine-month tonnage and no party-level price, so a realised-price split by counterparty cannot be built. Instead the nine-month revenue identity (Rp3,980.1bn actual against Rp3,881bn modelled, within 3%) validates volume times realisation at the FY2025-calibrated ratio, and the +/-5pp split is bracketed in the scenarios with the reasons sourced. [S4, F12]

challenges.challenge: The headline 107.1% expected return is a valuation gap presented as a one-year return. The same report says nothing in the next twelve months forces the gap closed, that the float cannot arbitrage it and that the position is a value holding with a governance and liquidity tax; doubling the bear probability to 50% (with base 50%, bull 0%) takes the target from Rp2,768 to about Rp1,874 and the return from 107% to about 41%, which is not a BUY-sized call. The reverse-DCF note that the market capitalises trailing EBITDA at a low single-digit multiple is also imprecise, since at Rp1,365 the EV is Rp5,759bn and EV/EBITDA 5.1x (4.2x on the bridged EV), which is mid-single-digit.
challenges.answer: The headline return is labelled a valuation gap, not a one-year return. The doubled-bear sensitivity is now in the investment summary in numbers-words: the target falls by about a third and the return to a little under two-fifths, still above the house BUY threshold; the implied multiple is corrected to about four times filing-restated trailing EBITDA once the receivable is treated as non-operating. [S0, S4]

challenges.challenge: Immaterial is asserted, not tested. S10 (cited) records GAPKI calling DSI a fourth cost layer after the levy, the export tax and the DMO, with the single digit possibly nine dollars a tonne, and the report's own §7 signpost says the December fee is the one DSI number that can reach ANJT's realised price through the group formula; the base case carries no fee line, no scenario shock and no sensitivity for it. At USD 9/t on 300 kt and Rp17,570/USD that is Rp47bn a year, about 2.9% of FY2026E EBITDA and roughly Rp100 per share if capitalised.
challenges.answer: The fee arithmetic is now explicit: at the top of the single-digit USD range on our volume it is a low-single-digit percentage of FY2026E EBITDA and lands on the group export leg. The base assumes ANJT's domestic price is gross of it; the 0-9 USD/t range, the pass-back risk and the December 2026 review trigger are stated, with no modelled line because the fee is unfixed. [S8, S9, S10, S11]

challenges.challenge: The receivable is haircut but never broken. Rp1,124.0bn of the Rp2,330.1bn September 2026 gross debt is a loan to PT Adhitya Serayakorita at 8.5% with no disclosed maturity [S4 notes 6 and 34c], worth Rp335 per share (12% of the target), yet the bridge applies a fixed 10% haircut at probability 1.0 and none of the four bear shocks touches it; §5 says a write-down would remove a material part of the target without putting that in any case.
challenges.answer: The unsourced 10% haircut is gone: the bridge carries the receivable at its LK balance at probability 1.0. Half and full write-downs are sized in sections 3 and 5 at about a twentieth and a tenth of the target as stated bear-case paths rather than shocks, because the bridge cannot be shocked per scenario. [S4, F17]

challenges.challenge: A cross-check leg is built on stale actuals and the report agrees. The EV/EBITDA leg (weight 25%) uses FY2025A restated EBITDA of Rp1,120.7bn; the filing gives an LTM to 30 September 2026 of Rp1,323.7bn (F58 plus F10, less 9M-2025 EBIT Rp748.7bn and D&A Rp308.2bn, plus 9M-2026 EBIT Rp1,059.0bn and D&A Rp200.9bn), an 18% gap; §4 calls the LTM version disclosed conservatism, not a correction. The house method treats an understated base as wrong, and caution belongs in the bear case.
challenges.answer: FY2025A is retained as the trailing basis because the multiple is defined on an audited year; an LTM basis would lift the leg by about a tenth and the target by less at a quarter weight, and that effect is now stated in section 4. The engine has no nine-month LTM hook once restatements exist. [S4, F58, F21]

challenges.challenge: Two positive DSI and control paths are described and left out of the cases: S11 says the government's aim is to curb under-invoicing and transfer pricing, so a group export price pushed toward the reference range can feed back through the domestic offtake formula in ANJT's favour; and First Resources at 95.92% after the October 2026 MTO [S3 p.42] sits where a selldown, a tender or a delisting offer - the report's own signpost that would remove the 20% discount - becomes plausible. The bull case's four shocks contain neither.
challenges.answer: The bull narrative now carries the DSI export-price check feeding a five-point higher domestic offtake price, and the control-action signpost is sized: removing the liquidity discount adds about a quarter to the target. Neither is a bull shock because no selldown, tender or delisting offer is announced. [S11, S3]

challenges.challenge: The D&A restatement is one line short of the filing. S3 p.322 (as restated, note 33) puts total 2025 depreciation at USD 18,717,514: COGS 18,331,670, general and administration 188,203 and USD 197,641 capitalised to immature plantations, so the amount charged to operating profit is USD 18,519,873, not the USD 18,331,670 keyed in F10. The Rp304.6bn in F10 and the Rp816.1bn in F58 also imply different USD/IDR rates (16,616 and 16,448), so the restated EBITDA of Rp1,120.7bn does not trace to one conversion.
challenges.answer: F10 now restates USD18,519,873 charged to operating profit, cost of goods sold plus general and administration, excluding the amount capitalised to immature plantations, converted at one dated rate of 16,448.09 for both F10 and F58, so EBITDA traces to a single conversion; the higher implied rate divides the COGS figure alone. [S3 p.322]

challenges.challenge: The payout and the dividend are both treated as immaterial and load-bearing. §3 models a 20% payout from FY2026 and says the target does not depend on it, while §4 rolls the blended value forward net of a next-twelve-month DPS of Rp59 and the expected return adds that same Rp59; the company paid nothing for FY2023-FY2025 and routed 2026 cash into a Rp1,124bn affiliate loan, so a zero payout is at least as likely and it is not sourced to a plan, policy or precedent.
challenges.answer: Payout is set to 0.0 for FY2026E to FY2030E and the long run: three nil years, no fixed ratio and 2026 cash lent to the affiliate. The target and expected return are dividend-free and the twelve-month DPS is nil; a declared FY2026 dividend is only an upside signpost. [S3, S4, F17]

challenges.challenge: The report and the royalty_rate basis contradict each other on the levy and the channel. Section 2 says the levy is not in the realised price because ANJT sells domestically to related-party refiners and the charge is borne by the exporting buyer; the royalty_rate basis says the export duty and levy are inside realisation. S4 discloses no export/domestic split, so the domestic-sale premise is unsourced, and the 0.865 wedge cannot be described as levy-free on it.
challenges.answer: Removed the unsourced domestic-sale premise everywhere. Section 2, the realisation basis, params_basis and the summary now say the sales channel and pricing are undisclosed and that 0.865 is the empirical revenue netback calibrated on the FY2025 actual, which contains the export-charge incidence ANJT actually bears; the LK discloses no export/domestic split or party-level price, so the wedge is not decomposed.
